name: India
summary: The Reserve Bank of India licenses and supervises commercial banks. In November 2025 it consolidated its instructions into entity-wise Directions (KYC, governance, responsible business conduct, outsourcing) and in July 2026 issued new fraud, cybersecurity and compliance Directions. FIU-IND receives reports under the PMLA 2002, SEBI governs certification of mutual fund sellers, CERT-In receives cyber incident reports, and the Data Protection Board enforces the DPDP Act 2023. Explicit training duties cover KYC/AML/CFT staff, cyber awareness (new recruits and annual for management), compliance culture, director training, certification for third-party product sellers and IIBF-certified recovery agents.

regulators.name: Reserve Bank of India
regulators.role: Banking regulator and supervisor: licensing, prudential, KYC/AML, conduct, fraud, cybersecurity and outsourcing Directions for commercial banks.

regulators.name: Financial Intelligence Unit - India
regulators.role: Receives cash, suspicious and other transaction reports under the PMLA 2002 and PML Rules 2005 and issues reporting formats and compliance orders.

regulators.name: Securities and Exchange Board of India
regulators.role: Securities regulator; requires NISM certification of people who sell or distribute mutual funds and other securities products, including bank staff.

regulators.name: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team
regulators.role: National cyber incident response agency under the IT Act 2000; receives mandatory cyber incident reports.

regulators.name: RBI Ombudsman (Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme)
regulators.role: Free alternate redress for customers of RBI-regulated entities whose complaints are rejected or unresolved; the 2026 Scheme replaced the 2021 Scheme.

regulators.name: Data Protection Board of India
regulators.role: Adjudicatory body under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 for personal data breaches and non-compliance.

regulators.name: Income Tax Department (Central Board of Direct Taxes)
regulators.role: Receives FATCA and CRS reports (Form 61B) from reporting financial institutions.

programs.title: India | PMLA 2002 and RBI KYC Directions: AML Awareness
audience: AML/CFT compliance staff and Principal Officer's team
programs.why: RBI's KYC Directions for commercial banks require an ongoing staff training programme on the bank's KYC/AML/CFT policy, with content tailored to frontline, compliance and onboarding staff. The policy itself implements the Prevention of Money-laundering Act 2002 and the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules 2005, so every relevant employee needs to understand money laundering risks, customer due diligence, record keeping and reporting to FIU-IND.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002
references.provision: Section 12 (reporting entity to maintain records and furnish information)
references.note: Banks, as reporting entities, must keep records that allow transactions to be reconstructed, report prescribed transactions to the Director, FIU-IND, keep client identity records, and keep that information confidential.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraphs 6-15 (KYC policy, ML/TF risk assessment, compliance, Designated Director, Principal Officer)
references.note: Banks need a Board-approved KYC policy, a documented ML/TF risk assessment reviewed at least annually, independent evaluation and audit of KYC compliance, and must name a Designated Director and a separate Principal Officer to FIU-IND and RBI.

programs.title: India | Countering Terrorist Financing under UAPA and the RBI KYC Directions
audience: AML/CFT compliance staff and Principal Officer's team
programs.why: Terrorist financing is within the KYC/AML/CFT policy on which RBI requires ongoing staff training. Staff must also apply the procedure under section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act 1967: no accounts for listed persons or entities, screening at onboarding and periodically, and immediate reporting of matches.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks must ensure no account is held for individuals or entities on the UN-designated terrorist lists and follow the Government's UAPA Order of 2 February 2021 (reproduced in Annex I) for freezing and reporting.

programs.title: India | Countering Proliferation Financing under the WMD Act Section 12A
audience: Trade finance and correspondent banking staff
programs.why: The KYC Directions require meticulous compliance with the section 12A WMD Act procedure: checking customers against the designated list at onboarding and periodically, not executing matching transactions and reporting matches immediately. RBI's express training duty is framed around the KYC/AML/CFT policy, so proliferation financing training is classed here as a competence need for the staff who run these checks.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks must follow the Ministry of Finance Order of 1 September 2023 on section 12A of the WMD Act (Annex II): no transactions with designated persons, screening at onboarding and periodically, and immediate reporting of any match with full particulars.

references.title: Section 12A of the WMD and their Delivery Systems (Prohibition of Unlawful Activities) Act, 2005 (FIU-IND legislation page)
references.note: FIU-IND lists the section 12A WMD Act procedure among the AML legislation reporting entities must follow.

programs.title: India | RBI Know Your Customer Directions and Customer Identification
programs.why: KYC is the core of RBI's AML/CFT regime. Banks must train staff on the KYC policy on an ongoing basis, with a particular focus on staff dealing with new customers, and video-based customer identification (V-CIP) may be run only by officials specially trained to perform liveness checks and spot manipulation or suspicious conduct.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks offering video-based customer identification must have a written workflow and allow only specially trained officials, able to check liveness and detect fraud or suspicious behaviour, to conduct the process.

programs.title: India | Customer Due Diligence under the PML Rules and RBI KYC Directions
programs.why: CDD (identifying and verifying customers and beneficial owners) is required by Rule 9 of the PML Rules and set out in detail in Chapter VI of the KYC Directions. RBI's ongoing training requirement expressly targets staff who deal with new customers, so CDD procedures must be taught to them.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (as amended)
references.note: Reporting entities must identify and verify clients and beneficial owners, may rely on third parties only under strict conditions while remaining responsible, and follow the regulator's guidelines under sub-rule (14).

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Chapter III (Customer Acceptance Policy) and Chapter VI (CDD procedure)
references.note: No anonymous or benami accounts, no account where CDD cannot be applied (with an STR considered), CDD before any account relationship, and CDD applied at the unique customer (UCIC) level.

programs.title: India | Enhanced Due Diligence for Higher-Risk Customers (RBI KYC)
programs.why: The KYC Directions require enhanced due diligence for higher-risk relationships, including non-face-to-face onboarding, and at least six-monthly review of risk categorisation. RBI requires KYC/AML/CFT training focused on onboarding and compliance staff, who apply EDD.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraphs 41 and 44 (risk-based monitoring; EDD for non-face-to-face onboarding)
references.note: Banks must review customer risk categorisation at least every six months, monitor high-risk accounts more intensively, and apply additional safeguards to non-face-to-face accounts until identity is verified face to face or by V-CIP.

programs.title: India | Ongoing Due Diligence and Periodic KYC Updation
programs.why: Banks must monitor transactions against the customer's profile, watch specified red-flag patterns, and periodically update KYC. Staff carrying out these duties fall within RBI's role-tailored KYC/AML/CFT training requirement.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Transactions must be consistent with what the bank knows of the customer; large or complex transactions, threshold breaches, high turnover and third-party cheque deposits followed by cash withdrawals need close monitoring, with monitoring intensity aligned to risk.

programs.title: India | Beneficial Ownership Identification (PML Rule 9(3))
programs.why: For legal-entity customers banks must identify the beneficial owner using the thresholds in Rule 9(3) of the PML Rules and take reasonable steps to verify identity. Staff opening such accounts are among those RBI expects to receive focused KYC/AML/CFT training.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (as amended)
references.note: Sets how the beneficial owner is determined for companies, partnerships, trusts and unincorporated bodies, by controlling ownership interest or control by other means.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Before opening an account for a non-natural person the bank must identify its beneficial owners and take all reasonable steps under Rule 9(3) to verify their identity.

programs.title: India | Politically Exposed Persons under the RBI KYC Directions
programs.why: Banks may serve PEPs only with risk management systems to detect them, reasonable steps to establish source of funds and wealth, senior management approval to open or continue the relationship and enhanced ongoing monitoring, extended to family members and close associates. Front-line and compliance staff applying these rules fall within RBI's targeted KYC/AML/CFT training.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Sets the PEP conditions: detection systems, source of funds and wealth, senior management approval (including when an existing customer becomes a PEP), enhanced monitoring, and coverage of relatives and close associates.

programs.title: India | Sanctions Screening against UN and Government of India Lists
programs.why: RBI requires banks to screen customers against the UNSC lists notified under UAPA and the WMD Act designated list, at onboarding and periodically, and to follow the Government's freezing and reporting orders. No separate sanctions course is prescribed; staff must be competent to apply the procedures.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraphs 56-57 (UAPA section 51A and WMD Act section 12A)
references.note: Banks must not hold accounts for listed terrorists or designated proliferators, must screen at onboarding and periodically, and must report matches immediately under the 2021 UAPA Order and 2023 WMD Order.

programs.title: India | Targeted Financial Sanctions: Freezing under UAPA Section 51A
audience: Principal Officer and AML/CFT compliance staff
programs.why: Targeted financial sanctions are implemented through the UAPA section 51A Order of 2 February 2021 and the WMD section 12A Order of 1 September 2023, which RBI requires banks to follow meticulously, including freezing and reporting to the nodal officers. Competence is required; no separate training mandate was found.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: The Directions reproduce the Government's UAPA and WMD procedures, which set out how matches are verified, funds frozen and nodal officers informed.

programs.title: India | Suspicious Transaction Reporting to FIU-IND
audience: AML/CFT compliance staff and Principal Officer's team
programs.why: Banks must report suspicious transactions to FIU-IND through the Principal Officer promptly once satisfied a transaction is suspicious, keep reports confidential (no tipping off), and must not treat a filed STR as a reason to restrict an account. RBI also deems a bank non-compliant if a money mule account was identified but no STR filed. Ongoing KYC/AML/CFT training is mandatory.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (as amended)
references.provision: Rule 8 (furnishing of information to the Director)
references.note: The Principal Officer files monthly cash and other prescribed reports by the 15th of the following month and furnishes suspicious transaction information promptly once satisfied it is suspicious; each day of delay is a separate violation.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraphs 52-55 and 68 (reporting to FIU-IND; money mules)
references.note: Banks report under Rule 7 and 8 using FIU-IND formats, keep the fact of reporting confidential, use alert-generating software, and must file STRs on accounts identified as money mules.

programs.title: India | Transaction Monitoring and Alert Review (RBI KYC)
programs.why: Banks must run software that raises alerts when transactions do not fit the customer's risk profile and must monitor specified high-risk patterns. RBI requires KYC/AML/CFT training focused on compliance staff, who investigate these alerts.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Specifies transaction types that must be monitored, encourages AI/ML tools for monitoring, and requires robust software that raises alerts on transactions inconsistent with the customer's risk category and profile.

programs.title: India | Correspondent Banking Due Diligence (RBI KYC)
audience: Correspondent banking and financial institutions teams
programs.why: Cross-border correspondent relationships need a Board-approved policy, information on the respondent's business, reputation, supervision and AML/CFT controls, senior management approval and documented responsibilities. Staff must be competent to perform this; no separate training duty applies.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Requires respondent due diligence, assessment of AML/CFT controls, prior senior management approval with Board post-facto approval, and clear documentation of each institution's responsibilities.

programs.title: India | ML/TF Risk Assessment and Risk-Based Approach
programs.why: Banks must periodically assess money laundering and terrorist financing risk across customers, geographies, products, services, transactions and channels, review it at least annually, report the outcome to the Board, and apply a risk-based approach. This calls for competent risk and compliance staff rather than a prescribed course.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: The internal risk assessment must consider sector vulnerabilities shared by the regulator, be documented and proportionate, be reviewed at least annually and be placed before the Board or a delegated committee.

programs.title: India | PMLA Record Keeping and Cash Transaction Reporting
programs.why: PMLA section 12 and the PML Rules require banks to keep transaction records for five years and identity records for five years after the relationship ends, to make them available to authorities quickly, and to file monthly cash transaction reports. The KYC training programme covers the policy generally; record-keeping competence is needed by the staff who maintain and retrieve records.

references.title: Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002
references.note: Requires records that allow reconstruction of transactions, reporting of prescribed transactions to FIU-IND, retention of client records, and a five-year retention period.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Five-year retention of transaction records and of identification records after the relationship ends, with records retrievable quickly for competent authorities.

programs.title: India | KYC/AML/CFT Training for Branch and Front-Desk Staff
programs.why: RBI's KYC Directions expressly require the training focus to differ for frontline staff and require banks to train front-desk staff specially to deal with issues that arise from customers' lack of awareness of KYC requirements.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 79 (Hiring of Employees and Employee training)
references.note: Banks must screen staff at hiring (Know Your Employee), aim for KYC/AML/CFT staff with integrity and sound knowledge, and run an ongoing training programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff onboarding new customers; front-desk staff need special training on customer-education issues.

programs.title: India | AML/CFT Oversight for the Board, Designated Director and Principal Officer
programs.why: The Board approves the KYC policy and the ML/TF risk assessment, a Board-nominated Designated Director answers for PMLA compliance, and the Principal Officer runs monitoring and reporting. These roles require knowledge of the regime; RBI's separate director-training duty (Miscellaneous Directions, paragraph 58) covers risk management generally rather than AML specifically.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Board-approved KYC policy, Board review of the risk assessment, quarterly audit notes to the Audit Committee, and the roles of the Designated Director and Principal Officer (who may not be the same person).

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks must design need-based training for directors on emerging developments and risk management and promote senior management awareness of security, risk and controls (not required for foreign banks).

programs.title: India | Prevention of Corruption Act 1988: Corporate Bribery Offence
audience: Relationship managers dealing with public bodies
programs.why: Since 2018 a commercial organisation commits an offence if a person associated with it bribes a public servant for its benefit, with a defence of adequate procedures. Staff of public sector banks are also public servants for the Act. No statutory training duty was verified, and the official text could not be opened (India Code blocks automated access), so this is classed as a competence need.

references.title: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (as amended in 2018)
references.note: Since the 2018 amendment a commercial organisation is liable when an associated person bribes a public servant for its benefit, with a defence of adequate procedures under guidelines the Central Government is to prescribe. Not opened: India Code blocks automated access.

programs.title: India | Fraud Risk Management and Card Fraud Control (RBI 2026)
audience: Card and digital payments fraud control teams
programs.why: RBI's 2026 fraud directions require a Board-approved fraud risk policy, an early warning signals framework, time-bound staff accountability and reporting to RBI and law enforcement. The digital payment security directions expressly require banks to educate and train staff, especially in fraud control, in fraud tools, investigation, rule setting and monitoring.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
references.provision: Paragraphs 5, 9, 11, 36 (fraud risk policy, organisation, staff accountability)
references.note: Banks need a Board-approved fraud risk policy covering prevention, early detection, investigation, staff accountability, recovery and reporting, a General Manager-level official responsible for fraud monitoring, and time-bound staff accountability examinations.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
references.note: Banks must educate staff, particularly in fraud control, about frauds and train them in fraud control tools, investigation techniques, customer and merchant education, card scheme rules, data analysis, liaison with law enforcement and rule-based monitoring.

programs.title: India | Compliance Culture and Mandatory Compliance Training (RBI)
programs.why: RBI's compliance function directions state that the duty to follow instructions meticulously must be reinforced for all staff through continuous and mandatory training on compliance matters, backed by staff accountability for breaches. Compliance staff should receive regular education on banking law, new products, governance and risk.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026
references.note: Compliance staff need suitable knowledge and regular education on laws, products and governance; all staff must be reminded periodically, through continuous and mandatory compliance training, of the need to comply, with disciplinary measures for non-compliance.

programs.title: India | Board Directors' Training and Familiarisation (RBI)
audience: Directors of public sector banks before induction
programs.why: RBI requires banks to provide need-based training to directors on emerging developments and challenges, and Boards to ensure directors are exposed to current management techniques, technology and risk systems. Public sector bank directors must be familiarised with the bank's functioning before induction.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks must design need-based training programmes for directors, promote senior management awareness of security, risk and controls in computerised environments, and keep directors current on management, technology, markets and risk (not insisted on for foreign banks).

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 9 (role of the Board of a PSB)
references.note: Each PSB director must be familiarised before induction with delegation of powers, strategy, organisation structure, controls and the market environment.

programs.title: India | Fit and Proper Criteria for Bank Directors (RBI Governance)
programs.why: Banks must obtain declarations from proposed directors and have the Nomination and Remuneration Committee test them against fit and proper criteria (qualification, expertise, track record, integrity), with continuing due diligence each year. This is a competence and suitability regime, not a training mandate.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraphs 23-25 (PSB elected directors) and 42-43 (private sector bank directors)
references.note: Requires declarations and undertakings in the Annex I format and NRC scrutiny against fit and proper criteria; private sector banks must also submit an annual certificate of continuing due diligence.

programs.title: India | Whistle Blower Mechanism for Fraud Concerns (RBI)
programs.why: RBI's fraud directions require a transparent mechanism under the bank's Whistle Blower Policy for examining complaints about possible fraud or suspicious activity in accounts. Staff need to know how to raise and handle such complaints; no separate training is prescribed.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
references.note: Whistle blower complaints about possible frauds or suspicious account activity must be examined and concluded through a transparent mechanism under the bank's Whistle Blower Policy.

programs.title: India | Internal Audit Staff Competence under Risk-Based Internal Audit
programs.why: RBI's internal audit directions require the audit department to have adequately skilled staff and state that internal auditors should be trained periodically on the bank's business, procedures, risk management, controls and MIS.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
references.note: Internal auditors need professional competence and should be trained periodically on business activities, operating procedures, risk management, control systems and MIS.

programs.title: India | Responsible Lending Conduct and Fair Practices (RBI)
audience: Digital lending and LSP oversight teams
programs.why: RBI's Responsible Business Conduct Directions consolidate lending conduct rules for commercial banks, including fair practices and digital lending through lending service providers. From 1 January 2027 a new section governs recovery conduct and requires a code of conduct for bank employees involved in recovery. The main Directions could not be opened (PDF host blocks automated access); competence is required.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025
references.note: Consolidates RBI's customer service, grievance redress, deposit account, financial inclusion and responsible lending conduct instructions for commercial banks. The full text is published only as a PDF on rbidocs.rbi.org.in, which blocks automated access, so it was not opened.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026
references.provision: New Section L, paragraphs 454A-454K, incl. 454I (training) and 454J (code of conduct) (effective 1 January 2027)
references.note: Replaces the recovery agent rules: recovery agencies may engage only agents holding the IIBF certificate earned by completing the Debt Recovery Agents training programme; the bank must adopt a code of conduct for recovery agents and its own staff, verify agents' antecedents, and publish its list of recovery agencies.

programs.title: India | Complaint Handling and the Internal Ombudsman (RBI 2026)
audience: Call centre and grievance redressal staff
programs.why: Banks must run an automated complaints management system and route partly resolved or rejected complaints to the Internal Ombudsman. RBI requires banks to use the analysis of complaints in training for frontline staff so that complaints are handled consistently, and card issuers must train call centre staff to handle and escalate complaints.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
references.note: Banks must feed analysis of complaints handled by the Internal Ombudsman, including root causes and remedies, into training programmes for frontline staff, with the IO involved where needed.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
references.note: Card issuers must train call centre staff adequately to handle and escalate complaints, with automatic escalation of unresolved complaints.

programs.title: India | RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme and Escalation
programs.why: Customers whose complaints are rejected or not resolved can approach the RBI Ombudsman. Banks must tell complainants about this option and give the Ombudsman their comments, including the Internal Ombudsman's view. A new Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2026 replaces the 2021 scheme; its text could not be opened, so this stays at competence.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
references.note: Banks must tell complainants of the option to approach the RBI Ombudsman when a complaint is rejected or partly resolved and must seek the Internal Ombudsman's comments when submitting to the RBI Ombudsman.

references.title: Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026
references.note: Listed on RBI's Schemes page alongside the 2021 Scheme it replaces; provides free alternate redress for customers whose complaints the bank has not resolved. The PDF sits on rbidocs.rbi.org.in, which blocks automated access, so it was not opened.

programs.title: India | Mis-selling Prevention and Third-Party Product Sales (RBI)
audience: Staff marketing third-party and wealth products
programs.why: RBI makes a certificate course mandatory before staff are posted to market third-party retail or wealth products, to curb mis-selling. From 1 January 2027 new conduct rules define mis-selling, require suitability checks, regulator-prescribed qualifications for sellers, training of sub-agents and refunds where mis-selling is proven. Card issuers must ensure agents are trained and do not mis-sell.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks must require staff to obtain a certificate before posting to treasury, risk management, accounting, credit management and marketing of third-party retail and wealth products, using IBA-recognised courses and any certification other financial regulators prescribe.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
references.note: Defines mis-selling, requires a Board policy on marketing and sale of own and third-party products with suitability and appropriateness criteria, training of DSA/DMA sub-agents, regulator-prescribed qualifications or certifications for staff and agents who sell, no incentives that encourage mis-selling, no compulsory bundling, and refunds where mis-selling is established.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
references.note: Card issuers must check through random checks and mystery shopping that agents are briefed and trained on soliciting customers, calling hours, privacy and product terms, and must stop mis-selling of cards.

programs.title: India | Customer Confidentiality and Data Protection (RBI and DPDP Act)
programs.why: Banks must keep customer information secret, use account opening data only with the customer's express consent for other purposes such as cross-selling, and protect customer data through a data leak prevention strategy. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 adds statutory duties for data fiduciaries; its text could not be opened. Staff must be competent; no specific training duty was verified.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.provision: Paragraph 63 (secrecy obligations and sharing of information)
references.note: Customer information arising from the banking relationship must be kept secret, and data collected at account opening must not be used for cross-selling or other purposes without the customer's express permission.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.note: Banks must have a comprehensive strategy to prevent loss or leakage of confidential business and customer data.

references.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
references.note: The Act requires data fiduciaries such as banks to protect personal data with reasonable security safeguards and to notify breaches; India Code also lists the DPDP Rules, 2025 (13 November 2025). India Code and MeitY block automated access, so the text was not opened.

programs.title: India | Recovery Agents and Debt Collection Conduct (RBI)
programs.why: From 1 January 2027 banks may use only recovery agents who hold the IIBF certificate after completing the Debt Recovery Agents training programme, and must adopt a code of conduct for recovery agents and their own employees. The current Responsible Business Conduct Directions (paragraphs to be replaced) also govern recovery until then.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fourth Amendment Directions, 2026
references.provision: New Section L, paragraphs 454A-454K, incl. 454I (training) and 454J (code of conduct) (effective 1 January 2027)
references.note: Replaces the recovery agent rules: recovery agencies may engage only agents holding the IIBF certificate earned by completing the Debt Recovery Agents training programme; the bank must adopt a code of conduct for recovery agents and its own staff, verify agents' antecedents, and publish its list of recovery agencies.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025
references.note: Consolidates RBI's customer service, grievance redress, deposit account, financial inclusion and responsible lending conduct instructions for commercial banks. The full text is published only as a PDF on rbidocs.rbi.org.in, which blocks automated access, so it was not opened.

programs.title: India | Product Suitability and Certified Sales Staff (RBI and SEBI)
audience: Staff selling mutual funds and investment products
Wealth and priority banking relationship managers
programs.why: Bank staff who sell mutual funds must hold NISM certification under SEBI's Certification Regulations and keep it current through continuing education. RBI separately requires certification before posting to third-party product sales, and from 2027 requires suitability and appropriateness assessments and regulator-prescribed qualifications for anyone selling own or third-party products.

references.title: Certification Programme for sale and/or distribution of mutual fund products (SEBI Circular Cir/IMD/DF/5/2010, with notification under regulation 3(1) of the Certification Regulations, 2007)
references.issuer: Securities and Exchange Board of India
references.note: From 1 June 2010 anyone employed or engaged in selling or distributing mutual fund products must pass the NISM certification examination and keep it current through Continuing Professional Education.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
references.note: Certification is mandatory before posting staff to marketing of third-party retail products and wealth management; where other financial regulators prescribe certification, that must be met.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Second Amendment Directions, 2026
references.note: Defines mis-selling, requires a Board policy on marketing and sale of own and third-party products with suitability and appropriateness criteria, training of DSA/DMA sub-agents, regulator-prescribed qualifications or certifications for staff and agents who sell, no incentives that encourage mis-selling, no compulsory bundling, and refunds where mis-selling is established.

programs.title: India | Information Security Awareness (RBI Cybersecurity Directions 2026)
audience: All bank staff and new recruits
Vendors and partners with access to bank systems
programs.why: RBI's 2026 cybersecurity and technology directions require banks to educate staff, vendors and partners on secure use of information assets and cyber risks, to make awareness programmes mandatory for all new recruits, to train lower and middle management annually and to evaluate staff awareness periodically.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.note: Banks must communicate security policies to staff, vendors and partners and educate them on cyber risks, give targeted training to key executive, operational and security roles, test awareness levels periodically, make cyber awareness mandatory for all new recruits, and train lower and middle management every year.

programs.title: India | Cybersecurity Awareness for Staff (RBI)
audience: All bank staff and new recruits
Key executive, operational and security administration staff
programs.why: Cybersecurity awareness is mandatory for every new recruit and must be repeated annually for lower and middle management, with targeted training for key personnel and a culture of reporting suspicious behaviour to the incident team.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.note: Banks must communicate security policies to staff, vendors and partners and educate them on cyber risks, give targeted training to key executive, operational and security roles, test awareness levels periodically, make cyber awareness mandatory for all new recruits, and train lower and middle management every year.

programs.title: India | Cyber Risk Oversight for the Board and Senior Management (RBI)
audience: IT Strategy Committee and Information Security Committee members
programs.why: Banks must keep the Board and senior management aware of evolving cyber threats and give them annual training on IT and cybersecurity risks and good practice, alongside governance structures such as the IT Strategy Committee and the Information Security Committee.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.note: The Board and senior management must be sensitised periodically to technology and cyber developments and receive annual training on IT and cybersecurity risks and evolving good practice.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.note: Senior management must ensure IT risk processes create a culture of IT risk awareness and cyber hygiene; the Information Security Committee approves and monitors security awareness initiatives.

programs.title: India | Phishing and Social Engineering Defence (RBI)
programs.why: Banks must subscribe to anti-phishing and anti-rogue app services, educate users about cyber risks, encourage reporting of suspicious behaviour, and warn customers never to share credentials or OTPs. Phishing-specific staff training is not separately prescribed but falls within the general awareness programme.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.provision: Paragraphs 148, 199-201 and 207 (anti-phishing; user awareness; customer education)
references.note: Requires anti-phishing takedown services, staff education on cyber risks with reporting of suspicious behaviour, and customer education on not sharing credentials, OTPs or PINs.

programs.title: India | Cyber Incident Response and Reporting to RBI and CERT-In
programs.why: Banks must provide specialised training to staff who handle cyber incidents, report incidents to RBI on the DAKSH platform within six hours of detection and also notify CERT-In proactively. CERT-In's 2022 directions separately set a six-hour reporting window (not opened).

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.note: Personnel handling cyber incidents must receive specialised training; incidents must be reported to RBI on DAKSH within six hours of detection and CERT-In notified proactively.

references.title: CERT-In Directions under section 70B(6) of the IT Act, 2000 (28 April 2022)
references.note: Require body corporates, including banks, to report listed cyber incidents to CERT-In within six hours of noticing them. The CERT-In host refuses automated connections, so the directions were not opened.

programs.title: India | Personal Data Breach Handling (DPDP Act and RBI)
programs.why: Data breaches in banks trigger RBI cyber incident reporting within six hours and, under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, breach duties to the Data Protection Board and affected individuals. The DPDP texts could not be opened, so no training duty was verified; competence is required.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.provision: Paragraphs 51 and 182 (data leak prevention; incident reporting)
references.note: Banks must prevent data leakage and report cyber incidents to RBI within six hours of detection.

references.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
references.note: The Act requires data fiduciaries such as banks to protect personal data with reasonable security safeguards and to notify breaches; India Code also lists the DPDP Rules, 2025 (13 November 2025). India Code and MeitY block automated access, so the text was not opened.

references.title: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
references.issuer: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
references.note: MeitY copy of the Act; the host returned 403 to automated access, so it was not opened.

programs.title: India | Technology Resilience and Business Continuity (RBI 2026)
programs.why: RBI's 2026 directions require BCP and disaster recovery policies based on recognised good practice, defined recovery objectives and periodic testing, as part of a broader technology risk and resilience framework. Staff must be competent; no separate training requirement applies beyond the general cyber awareness programme.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.provision: Paragraphs 163-164 and 195 (BCP and DR; recovery metrics)
references.note: BCP and DR policy should follow good practice such as ISO 22301 and support rapid recovery; banks must set recovery point and time objectives for critical systems.

programs.title: India | IT and Cyber Risk Management Framework (RBI 2026)
audience: IT risk and information security teams
programs.why: The 2026 directions replaced RBI's earlier IT governance and cybersecurity framework instructions with a single framework covering governance, IT and cyber risk assessment, controls, a security operations centre and IS audit. When assessing control effectiveness banks must consider qualified resources and training programmes; SOC staff must be adequately trained.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.note: Sets IT governance roles, requires control evaluations to consider qualified staff and training programmes, and repeals the earlier IT governance and cybersecurity framework instructions for commercial banks.

programs.title: India | Managing Risks in Outsourcing (RBI 2025)
audience: IT outsourcing and cloud governance teams
programs.why: Banks need a Board-approved outsourcing policy, Board and Audit Committee oversight of material outsourcing, due diligence, audit and exit strategies for financial and IT outsourcing. This requires competent oversight staff rather than a prescribed course.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
references.note: The Board-approved outsourcing policy must set selection criteria, materiality parameters and delegation; IT outsourcing policies must include tested exit strategies to ensure continuity.

programs.title: India | Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (RBI 2026)
programs.why: BCP and DR capabilities must be designed for rapid recovery and tested, with response plans that cover a range of scenarios. Staff must know their roles, but RBI prescribes no separate BCM training.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
references.provision: Paragraphs 163-164 and 177 (BCP and DR; incident scenarios)
references.note: Requires BCP/DR policies based on good practice and response plans ready for varied incident scenarios with coordinated communication.

programs.title: India | Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (POSH) Act 2013
programs.why: The POSH Act requires every employer to set up an Internal Committee and, under section 19, to hold workshops and awareness programmes for employees at regular intervals and orientation for Internal Committee members. That would justify a mandatory classification, but the official text on India Code could not be opened (automated access blocked), so it is held at competence until checked.

references.title: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013
references.note: The Act requires employers to constitute an Internal Committee and, under section 19, to sensitise employees through workshops and awareness programmes at regular intervals and to run orientation programmes for Internal Committee members. India Code blocks automated access, so this was not confirmed against the text.

programs.title: India | FATCA Registration, Due Diligence and Reporting
programs.why: Banks must register with US authorities and obtain a GIIN, decide whether they are Reporting Financial Institutions under the income-tax rules, register on the Income Tax Department e-filing portal and file Form 61B using the Designated Director's digital signature. Competence is needed; no training duty was found.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks not yet registered must register under the India-US IGA and obtain a GIIN, with registration steps for overseas branches in Model 1 and Model 2 jurisdictions.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks must apply Income Tax Rules 114F-114H, register as Reporting Financial Institutions on the e-filing portal and submit Form 61B or a nil report signed by the Designated Director.

programs.title: India | Common Reporting Standard Due Diligence and Reporting
programs.why: CRS reporting follows the same income-tax rules and Form 61B process as FATCA. Staff collecting self-certifications and preparing reports need competence; no training duty was found.

references.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
references.note: Banks must apply Income Tax Rules 114F-114H, register as Reporting Financial Institutions on the e-filing portal and submit Form 61B or a nil report signed by the Designated Director.

notes: On 28 November 2025 RBI repealed its earlier circulars and master directions for commercial banks and replaced them with entity-wise Directions; the KYC Master Direction of 2016 was replaced by the Commercial Banks - Know Your Customer Directions, 2025 (updated to 1 October 2026; amended 18 September 2026 for FPI document certification).

On 31 July 2026 RBI issued new Directions for commercial banks on fraud risk management, cybersecurity and technology risk (replacing the 2023 IT Governance Master Direction and the cyber security framework), digital payment security controls, compliance function and internal audit, all effective on issue.

Internal Ombudsman Directions 2026 (14 January 2026) replaced the 2023 IO Master Direction; the Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026 replaces the 2021 Scheme (RBI's file name indicates 1 July 2026; scheme text not opened).

Responsible Business Conduct amendments effective 1 January 2027: comprehensive mis-selling and third-party product rules (Second Amendment, 15 June 2026) and new recovery agent rules with mandatory IIBF certification (Fourth Amendment, 6 August 2026).
The PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules were last amended in 2023 (FIU-IND's consolidated text cites the Third Amendment Rules, 2023).

The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025 with phased commencement; most data fiduciary obligations are reported to apply from May 2027. Neither the Rules nor the Act could be opened (MeitY and India Code block automated access).
Not verified: the Income-tax Act, 2025 is reported to replace the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026, which may renumber the FATCA/CRS rules; RBI's KYC Directions (October 2026) still cite Rules 114F-114H.
RBI full-text PDFs on rbidocs.rbi.org.in return a bot-check page; where RBI publishes Directions only as PDF (e.g. Responsible Business Conduct) the text was not opened.
